\newcommand{\rzero}{{\mathcal R}_0}

The recent paper by @sidhuAttenuationVirulenceYersinia2025 documented the repeated emergence of reduced-virulence strains of *Y. pestis*[^pla-reduced] across all three plague pandemics.
We have been working to develop and test a mathematical model that formalizes the verbal arguments that we gave in @sidhuAttenuationVirulenceYersinia2025, as follows:

[^pla-reduced]: these strains are called "*pla*-reduced" or "*pla*-depleted", for a reduction in copy number of the pPCP1 plasmid carrying *pla*, which encodes the plasminogen activator Pla. 

> Our *in vivo* results showed that *pla*-reduced, attenuated strains that carry a
> single copy of the *pla* gene remain fully capable of causing lethal bubonic
> infections, inducing full blown pneumonia (as well as septicemia), contrary to
> engineered strains that lack *pla* or have no Pla activity [@Sode+1992; @Sebb+2006; @Lath+2007; @Caul+2014; @Bane+2020]. However,
> selection for *pla* depletion likely occurred in the context of bubonic plague, as it
> was the only form of the disease for which we observed an effect on virulence. Knowing
> that *pla*-reduced strains take longer than *pla*-WT strains to kill their host in our
> *in vivo* experiments, it may initially appear that the selection for *pla* depletion
> reflects a classical transmission-virulence trade-off [@Bram+2021; @Cres+2016; @LensMay1994; @Lens1988]. However, bubonic
> plague is primarily transmitted from one host to another during a very short
> late-stage high bacteremia, which leads to the death of the initial host and movement
> of their infected fleas to another host [@KeelGill2000; @Lora+2005; @Hinn+2017]. Because fatal bacteremia enhances
> transmission, the reduced virulence and higher host survival time due to *pla*
> depletion would seemingly decrease overall transmission and hence be selectively
> disadvantageous.

> Instead, we suggest that these data support models of epidemic burnout [@Pars+2024] in which
> pathogen attenuation enables disease persistence in small and fragmented populations
> through frequent, reinitiated epidemics after population recovery. Indeed, modeling
> has suggested that both metapopulation structure and partial population immunity could
> account for plague persistence in the modern plague Malagasy foci [@Gasc+2013]. Sylvatic
> rodent reservoirs are responsible for the long-term persistence of *Y. pestis* in
> nature [@Davi+2004], whereas multiple peridomestic rodent species, including black rats, play
> the role of amplification hosts [@Zepp+2016]. We focused on black rats (and their associated
> fleas) because they represent recognized drivers of plague epidemics in urban locales
> [@Zepp+2016; @Gage2012; @EiseGage2008; @GageKoso2005; @WHO1953; @Rahe+2010; @Raha+2003]. The highly virulent *pla*-WT strain that generates frequent septicemia with a
> greater reproduction number than the *pla*-reduced strain would be selectively
> advantageous in the large, fecund naïve [@Rahe+2010; @Wu+2008], highly susceptible [@EiseGage2008; @GageKoso2005; @WHO1953; @Andri2012; @Andr+2018; @Toll+2010],
> and well-connected metapopulations of rats that likely characterized the early phases
> of pandemics and where susceptible hosts were easily replenished. However, after
> reductions in the size and density of peridomestic rat populations during repeated
> epidemic waves, we hypothesize that there was selection at the metapopulation level
> for *pla*-reduced strains. The high rat mortality that likely accompanied documented
> massive human mortality during the Black Death and the subsequent decennial epidemics
> likely led to low rodent densities for long periods of time. Indeed, prairie dog
> colonies can take years to recover after epizootics with high mortality rates of >95%
> [@CullWill2001]. Human population sizes in Europe were also reduced by ~30 to 50% during the
> Black Death and remained low until the mid-16th century [@BardDupa1997; @WrigScho1982], likely affecting
> human-rat plague cycles. This decline in the density of susceptible hosts and their
> increasing population fragmentation about a century into the second pandemic (~1420
> CE) may thus have created an environment that favored *pla*-reduced, attenuated
> strains of *Y. pestis* over their more virulent *pla*-WT relatives. Specifically, a
> decreased mortality rate and longer time to host death would allow for continued
> movement of rats between existing populations, now more distantly spaced than early in
> the pandemic, allowing for the continued persistence, and hence increased
> transmission, of *Y. pestis* and the subsequent slow burn of the epidemic. Although
> metapopulation or landscape-level mechanisms for plague persistence have been
> suggested [@KeelGill2000; @davisabundance2008; @Schm+2012], we are not aware of previous hypotheses concerning the
> metapopulation-level selection of *Y. pestis*, though the concept of
> metapopulation-level selection for pathogen virulence or predator efficiency is well
> established in theoretical ecology [@claessenEvolution1995; @bootsSmall1999; @Pels+2002].

We were inspired by our work on epidemic burnout (@Pars+2024), which suggests that lowering within-population $\rzero$ (from $\approx 2$) could decrease the probability of burnout in the trough after the initial introduction of plague into a population. However, the story is more complicated.

* **demographic models matter**: @Pars+2024 considered only the case where hosts are replenished at a constant rate (i.e., a constant absolute birth rate), which is reasonable for a disease with low impact on population size. For rat populations affected by plague, however, a logistic growth model (*per capita* birth rate/susceptible replenishment rate decreasing with population size; absolute birth rate highest for intermediate population size) is more reasonable. We also considered a different range of parameter values: the ratio of disease generation interval to replenishment time scale is vastly different for *Y. pestis* in rats ($\approx 0.1$--$0.2$) as compared to acute infectious disease (e.g. flu, measles) in humans ($< 0.001$).
* **simple metapopulation models may not work**: in stochastic simulation models of plague in rat metapopulations, we find a 'ratchet' effect. Because (1) persistence is extremely likely once an epidemic survives through the first trough and (2) a higher-$\rzero$, 'wild type' strain will outcompete a lower-$\rzero$, *pla*-reduced strain within a patch, the proportion of patches occupied by the wild type typically grows slowly (but irreversibly) over time. One might concoct a scenario where the accumulation is slow enough to see metapopulation-level persistence of both strains over a long time frame, but it is hard to explain takeover by a *pla*-reduced strain. Because burnout is driven by epidemic overshoot, which in turn depends on a large initial susceptible population, previous colonization of a patch by a *pla*-reduced strain actually makes it *easier* (by reducing the susceptible population size) for a wild-type strain to invade and persist in the patch.
* **seasonality may change the story**: we know that second-pandemic outbreaks in humans were seasonal [@krauerInfluenceTemperatureSeasonality2021]. Preliminary tests suggest that adding a seasonally varying transmission rate allows long-term, stable, intermediate patch occupancy for a single strain (rather than a ratcheted increase in occupancy as in non-seasonal models). Thus such models may admit a scenario as we originally envisioned where a *pla*-reduced strain becomes evolutionarily dominant as patch size and connectivity decrease over time. ## open questions/questioning assumptions

* is the enhanced possibility of colonization (through increased survival while infected), as mentioned in @sidhuAttenuationVirulenceYersinia2025, sufficient to give *pla*-reduced strains an evolutionary advantage when patches are small and far apart?
* how do the changes in *pla* copy number affect rat-to-flea transmission probabilities? (not necessarily an experiment anyone wants to do ...)
* should we be considering possibilities other than the classic rat-flea transmission cycle? (evolution in humans, e.g. importance of human ectoparasite/pneumonic transmission modes?)
* how can historical or ancient-DNA evidence shed light on the ancient ecology of plague and its hosts? e.g.
   * evidence of host (rat) coevolution with plague
   * finding out more about the sylvatic cycle
   * proxies for historical rat populations
   * ancient polymorphisms/substitutions that are connected to *Y. pestis* loci that have known phenotypic effects in its hosts or vectors (based on current-day empirical studies) [e.g. @@Hinn+2017]
   
The general point is that ancient DNA can tell us an astonishing amount about organism-level biology, but ecology (starting with mechanisms of transmission and working up to population-level effects) is harder (although not impossible; for example, coalescent methods tell us about population history).
